description: We are a group of students from Ramazan Yaman Science Highschool interested in NASA, space and technology.
summary: We made a GIS for Mars. Our GIS has many features regarding Mars' surface. You can check and make your route on the point we selected in Mars (Arcadia Planitia). You can check many conditions in the Mars surface by using and exploring layer maps (GeoTIFF).
details:
Our project first loads a leaflet map version of Mars' surface. We used Mars Trek and other sources the challenge officially provided us to access the GeoTIFF files for thermal, optical, geophysical, dust, slope datas.

We chose a strategically advanced place in Mars for our route. We decided to choose the Arcadia Planitiia region because it met our criteria, and we selected a crater located approximately at 46.56° North Latitude and 173° West Longitude. The crater's proximity to the poles and its very low slope played a major role in our selection. Furthermore, thanks to the SHADAR system, we discovered a large mass of water ice beneath the crater. The potential use of this water ice as both a hydrogen source and a natural radiation source was another important factor in our choice. Additionally, the region's volcanic rock composition, allowing for rock analysis, and its soft ground are among its advantages.

The Martian surface generally consists of rugged, mountainous, and sloping terrain; these geological features create problems for landing on the Martian surface. However, for the crater we chose, the 20.7 km MOLA profile has an average absolute slope of 0.75°, with the steepest section being approximately 4°. The low-sloping, wide base provides a suitable ground for landing and surface movement.

On the Martian surface, most rocks and minerals are covered by dust, regolith, and erosion products. Therefore, scientific sampling requires searching for exposed materials and mineral signatures in the correct areas. Which units can be sampled depends on the geological diversity of the region. In our chosen crater, fresh crater ejecta and exposed materials on the slopes offer sampling targets for mineral and ice traces. The region contains both volcanic and ice-related geological units in the same area.

Mars has no global magnetic field and its atmosphere is very thin. Therefore, the surface is directly exposed to galactic cosmic rays (GCR) and solar particle incidents (SPE). While on Earth the magnetosphere deflects most of these particles, Mars lacks this protection. For this reason, radiation is a very significant danger. The average elevation of the crater we have chosen is -3,991 m. The low elevation increases the atmospheric column above the surface and reduces the amount of radiation reaching the surface. Therefore, this region is safer in terms of radiation compared to other areas.
dataRefs: The main source for our Mars map layers. It presents multi-mission data in one place.
NASA Goddard’s Mars Explorer app. It helped us understand atmospheric and environmental conditions.
The official archive for MRO camera images such as CTX. Used for high-resolution surface imagery.
NASA’s On-Line Tool for the Assessment of Radiation in Space. Used to calculate the radiation an astronaut would be exposed to.
projectRefs: Contains Mars elevation and topography data. It is the basis of our slope analysis.
Plasma and particle environment data. Used for radiation and space weather safety.
Spectral data. Used to understand surface mineral composition and to define scientific targets.
Geological maps and scientific publications. Used to verify the geology of the region.
